description: Curated, voice-neutral cultivation issue reference that grounds StoneHead's diagnostic answers. Differentiators are the payload. Facts favor university extension and GrowWeedEasy; researched/confirmed before authoring. Contains NO per-strain grow-trait data, NO photo/vision data, and NO live-data dependencies (all deferred to Phase 2/3).

field_notes.confused_with: issue ids this is commonly mistaken for; each has a matching differentiator
field_notes.differentiators: one {vs, tell} per confused_with id — the disambiguating observation
field_notes.fix: corrective DIRECTION only (no brand dosing); names what to check first
field_notes.escalate: true = give the careful answer AND flag it's serious (not 'refuse')
field_notes.is_normal: true = reassurance entry (a healthy plant people panic over)

issues.name: Nitrogen Deficiency
user_phrases: bottom leaves turning yellow
lower leaves yellowing and falling off
leaves going pale from the bottom up
symptoms: uniform yellowing (chlorosis) starting on lower/older leaves
yellowing progresses upward over time
older leaves may drop
likely_causes: genuinely under-feeding / nitrogen too low
soil base nutrients depleted in late veg
pH out of range blocking nitrogen uptake (lockout, not a true shortage)

differentiators.tell: Fade is expected in roughly the last 2 weeks of flower and sweeps the whole canopy as the plant cannibalizes itself; a true deficiency hits earlier and faster.
If feeding is already adequate but it keeps spreading, suspect pH — check runoff/res pH BEFORE adding more nitrogen.
Mg is interveinal (green veins, yellow between) usually mid-plant; N is uniform yellowing, low-and-upward.
Overwatering yellowing comes with droop and constantly-wet medium; N yellowing tracks feeding/age, not soil moisture.

clarifying_questions: What week are you in?
What are you feeding and how often?
Soil or coco/hydro — and do you know your runoff/res pH?
issues.fix: If genuinely under-fed and NOT in late flower, raise nitrogen toward label strength and recheck in a few days. Confirm pH is in range first so you're not chasing lockout. Don't overcorrect — nitrogen toxicity is its own problem.

issues.name: Nitrogen Toxicity / Overfeeding ("The Claw")
user_phrases: leaf tips clawing down
dark green leaves curling under
leaves look really dark and shiny and bent
tips pointing down like talons
symptoms: very dark green, glossy/waxy leaves
leaf tips bend and curl downward ("claw")
clawing most pronounced on upper growth
likely_causes: too much nitrogen / overall nutrients too strong
running a high-nitrogen veg formula into flower
salt buildup in the root zone

differentiators.tell: Nute burn shows burnt/brown crispy leaf TIPS; N toxicity shows dark-green clawing without the burnt tip (they often appear together when feeding is too strong).
Overwatering droops the WHOLE leaf downward from the stem and pairs with a wet medium; the claw is the leaf TIPS curling under on dark-green, firm leaves.
Heat curls leaf EDGES upward (tacoing); N toxicity curls leaf tips DOWNward.

clarifying_questions: What strength are you feeding versus the label, and what's your runoff/res EC/PPM if you measure it?
Are the leaves dark green and glossy, and is it the tips or the whole leaf curling?
issues.fix: Ease back nutrient strength (especially nitrogen) toward or below label, and flush the medium with pH-balanced water if salts have built up. Confirm pH so you're reading the plant correctly. Damaged leaves won't un-claw, but new growth should come in normal.

issues.name: Phosphorus Deficiency
user_phrases: leaves turning dark with purple stems
lower leaves bluish-green with bronze spots
stems going red or purple
older leaves dark and dull
symptoms: older/lower leaves go dark bluish-green and dull
bronze/brown blotches on older leaves
petioles/stems may redden or purple
likely_causes: phosphorus genuinely low (more common in flower when demand rises)
pH out of range — P uptake is poor in cold or low/high pH (lockout)
cold root zone reducing P availability

differentiators.tell: K deficiency burns leaf MARGINS/tips of older leaves; P deficiency darkens the whole older leaf and adds bronze blotching, often with reddened stems.
P is one of the first things locked out by cold or off pH — check medium temperature and runoff/res pH before adding more P.

clarifying_questions: What week of flower are you in, and how cold does the root zone get at night?
What's your runoff/res pH?
issues.fix: If pH and root-zone temperature are in range and it's still spreading, raise phosphorus toward label (bloom-stage feeds run higher P). Warm cold roots first — cold alone can cause this without any true shortage.
issues.confidence_note: Reddish/purple stems and petioles can also be genetic or cold-driven rather than a true phosphorus shortage; treat stem color as a weak signal on its own.

issues.name: Potassium Deficiency
user_phrases: edges of older leaves turning brown and crispy
burnt-looking leaf margins on lower leaves
yellowing tips and edges down low
older leaves rusting at the edges
symptoms: yellowing then browning of MARGINS and tips on older/lower leaves
edges look scorched/crispy while leaf center stays greener
sometimes rusty spotting on older leaves
likely_causes: potassium genuinely low (demand rises in flower)
pH out of range limiting K uptake (lockout)
nutrient imbalance from heavy bloom boosters

differentiators.tell: Both burn leaf edges/tips — but nute burn comes from OVER-feeding and hits the whole plant including upper/newer leaves; K deficiency is UNDER-supply and concentrates on OLDER/lower leaves.
K deficiency is edge/margin burn on older leaves; P deficiency darkens the whole older leaf with bronze blotching and reddened stems.
Check runoff/res pH before adding K — off pH mimics the same marginal burn.

clarifying_questions: Are the burnt edges only on the lower/older leaves, or all over the plant?
How strong are you feeding, and what's your runoff/res pH?
issues.fix: If it's older leaves only and feeding is modest, nudge potassium toward label and recheck. Confirm pH first. If the whole plant including new growth is burning at the tips, treat it as overfeeding instead and back off.

issues.name: Calcium Deficiency
user_phrases: new top leaves spotty and twisted
brown spots on the newer leaves
new growth curling and deformed
weak floppy stems on new growth
brown spots with yellow around them on the leaves
symptoms: small brown/rusty spots on NEW/upper leaves, often at edges
new growth distorted, curled, or hooked ("parachuting" tips)
weak stems; poor root development in bad cases
likely_causes: calcium low — common with soft/filtered/RO water
pH out of range blocking calcium uptake (lockout)
coco coir without added cal-mag

differentiators.tell: Location is the tell: calcium hits NEW/upper growth (immobile); magnesium hits OLD/lower leaves (mobile) with interveinal yellowing.
Both affect new growth — but iron is clean interveinal yellowing on new leaves, while calcium adds brown edge spotting and twisted/distorted new growth.
Calcium uptake is very pH-sensitive — check runoff/res pH before dosing cal-mag.

clarifying_questions: Are you using RO, filtered, or soft water, or growing in coco?
Is it the newest top growth that's affected, and what's your pH?
issues.fix: If on RO/soft water or in coco, add a cal-mag supplement toward label and correct pH (calcium locks out off-range). Old damaged leaves won't recover; new growth should come in clean within about a week.
issues.confidence_note: Calcium and magnesium are frequently deficient together (hence 'cal-mag'); if symptoms appear on both new and old growth, treat them as a pair.

issues.name: Magnesium Deficiency
user_phrases: yellow between the veins on lower leaves
green veins but yellow in between
rusty spots on the older leaves
lower leaves striping yellow
symptoms: interveinal chlorosis on OLDER/lower leaves (green veins, yellow between)
rusty/brown flecks on affected older leaves
leaf tips/edges may curl up; progresses upward if unfixed
likely_causes: magnesium low — common with soft/filtered/RO water
pH out of range blocking Mg uptake (lockout)
coco coir without added cal-mag

differentiators.tell: N is UNIFORM yellowing of older leaves; Mg keeps the veins green and yellows BETWEEN them (interveinal).
Same interveinal pattern, opposite location: Mg shows on OLD/lower leaves (mobile), iron on NEW/upper growth (immobile).
Mg is interveinal yellowing on old leaves; calcium is brown spotting and distorted growth on NEW leaves.
Check runoff/res pH first — low pH commonly drives an Mg-looking deficiency without a true shortage.

clarifying_questions: Is the yellowing between the veins on the LOWER leaves while veins stay green?
RO/soft water or coco — and what's your pH?
issues.fix: Correct pH first, then add cal-mag (or Epsom salts / dolomite lime in soil) toward label if on RO/soft water or coco. Affected old leaves stay marked; new growth should green up. Don't overcorrect.

issues.name: Iron Deficiency
user_phrases: new top growth bright yellow
newest leaves yellow with green veins
tops went pale/yellow almost white
upper new leaves yellowing between veins
symptoms: interveinal-to-uniform yellowing on the NEWEST/upper leaves
veins may stay greener than the surrounding tissue
new growth can look pale, almost bright/lime
likely_causes: pH too high (most common trigger — iron locks out above range)
overwatering / poor root function reducing iron uptake
iron genuinely low (less common; often a pH problem in disguise)

differentiators.tell: Location is the tell: iron is on the NEWEST/upper growth (immobile); Mg is on OLD/lower leaves (mobile).
Both hit new growth, but iron is clean interveinal/uniform yellowing; calcium adds brown edge spots and twisted new leaves.
Iron is the classic high-pH lockout — check pH FIRST; correcting pH usually fixes it without adding iron.

clarifying_questions: Is it the very newest top growth that's pale/yellow?
What's your pH, and have you been watering heavily?
issues.fix: Check and correct pH first — iron is overwhelmingly a high-pH lockout, not a true shortage. Let an overwatered medium dry back so roots can work. Only supplement iron (cal-mag includes a trace) if pH is dialed and it persists.

issues.name: Nutrient Burn (Overfeeding / Burnt Tips)
user_phrases: burnt brown tips on the leaves
leaf tips going yellow then crispy
tips look burnt all over the plant
edges curling and browning
symptoms: leaf TIPS yellow then turn brown/tan and crispy
burn creeps inward along margins if it worsens
affects leaves across the whole plant, including newer growth; leaves can look dark green
likely_causes: nutrients mixed too strong / feeding too heavily
salt buildup in the root zone
"hot" soil or bloom boosters; pH off, causing accumulation

differentiators.tell: Same root cause (too much food). Burn = crispy brown tips; N toxicity = dark-green downward clawing. They commonly show together.
Nute burn hits tips/edges across the plant; light burn bleaches/yellows the UPPER leaves closest to the lamp and tracks distance from the light, not feeding.
K deficiency is edge burn on OLDER leaves from UNDER-feeding; nute burn is OVER-feeding and hits new growth too.
Off pH causes salts to accumulate and burn even at normal doses — check pH/runoff EC before assuming the dose is too high.

clarifying_questions: How strong are you feeding versus the label, and do you measure runoff/res EC/PPM?
Are the burnt tips all over the plant, or only on the older lower leaves?
issues.fix: Flush the medium with pH-balanced water to clear salts, then resume feeding at reduced strength (start lower for autos/seedlings) and build up slowly. Burnt tips won't heal; the goal is clean new growth.

issues.name: pH Out of Range / Nutrient Lockout
user_phrases: multiple deficiencies at once
tried adding nutrients but it keeps getting worse
leaves doing weird stuff even though I feed
lots of different colors and spots showing up
could this be a pH problem
lower leaves yellowing, is it feeding or pH
is my pH off
symptoms: deficiency-style symptoms (yellowing, spotting, interveinal) despite adequate feeding
several deficiencies appearing together
symptoms persist or worsen after adding more nutrients
likely_causes: root-zone pH outside the uptake range (soil ~6.2-7.0; coco/hydro ~5.5-6.5)
salt buildup shifting medium pH over time
tap/source water pH not adjusted before feeding

differentiators.tell: If feeding is already adequate and it keeps spreading, it's likely pH locking out N rather than a true shortage — adding more N won't help until pH is fixed.
Low pH frequently mimics Mg deficiency; correcting pH resolves the 'Mg' look without dosing Mg.
Calcium uptake is very pH-sensitive — an off pH reads as a calcium problem; check pH before adding cal-mag.
Iron locks out at HIGH pH specifically — pale new tops with high pH is lockout, not a true iron shortage.
Off pH reproduces the same marginal burn; rule pH out before dosing K.

clarifying_questions: What's the pH of your runoff (soil/coco) or reservoir (hydro)?
Soil, coco, or hydro — and are you pH-adjusting your water before feeding?
issues.fix: Measure and correct pH into range for your medium BEFORE adding any nutrients (this is the single most important check behind the whole deficiency cluster). In soil/coco, flush with correctly pH'd water if salts have built up, then feed in range.

issues.name: Overwatering
user_phrases: plant drooping after I water
leaves droopy and the soil is still wet
droopy and the pot feels heavy
leaves curling down and looking sad
symptoms: drooping leaves that feel FIRM/swollen and curl down from the stem
medium stays wet; pot feels heavy long after watering
can yellow and stunt growth as roots suffocate
likely_causes: watering too OFTEN (not letting the medium dry back)
poor drainage / dense, water-holding medium
pot too big for the plant; cool, humid conditions slowing water use

differentiators.tell: Check the medium: overwatering = WET and pot HEAVY, leaves firm/swollen; underwatering = DRY and pot LIGHT, leaves limp/papery. Droop alone can't tell them apart.
Overwatering yellowing comes WITH droop and a constantly-wet medium; N-def yellowing tracks feeding/age on a normally-watered plant.
The claw is leaf TIPS curling under on dark-green leaves; overwatering droops the WHOLE leaf and pairs with a wet medium.
Root rot is where chronic overwatering has gone — brown, soft, foul-smelling roots. Overwatering is the cause; root rot is the damage.
Heat curls leaf edges UP and eases when it cools; overwatering droop tracks a wet medium regardless of temperature.
Overwatering droops the whole plant and eases as the pot dries out. Broad/russet mites twist and gloss only the newest top growth and keep getting worse no matter how you water.

clarifying_questions: Is the medium wet and the pot heavy right now, or dry and light?
How often are you watering, and does the pot have drainage holes?
issues.fix: Let the medium dry back before watering again, and water on plant demand (pot weight) rather than a schedule. Improve drainage/airflow and match pot size to the plant. If roots are already brown and slimy, treat it as root rot.

issues.name: Underwatering
user_phrases: leaves drooping and the soil is bone dry
wilting and the pot feels really light
my plant is drooping and wilting
limp lifeless leaves
leaves perk up fast after I water
symptoms: drooping leaves that feel LIMP, thin, papery, brittle
medium dry and light; may crack or pull away from the pot
perks up within hours of watering
likely_causes: not watering enough / letting the medium go bone dry
medium gone hydrophobic (water runs down the sides, not into the root ball)
plant outgrew its pot and drinks faster than expected

differentiators.tell: Check the medium: underwatering = DRY, pot LIGHT, leaves limp/papery; overwatering = WET, pot HEAVY, leaves firm/swollen.
Heat wilt curls edges up and recovers when it cools even with moisture present; underwatering recovers only after you actually water.
Chronic dryness can crisp leaf edges like nute burn — but the medium is bone dry and the pot is light, versus a salt problem you'd see on a normally-watered plant.

clarifying_questions: Is the medium dry and the pot noticeably light?
When you water thoroughly, does it perk back up within a few hours?
issues.fix: Water slowly and thoroughly until you get a little runoff, re-wetting a hydrophobic medium gradually (several passes). Then water on demand by pot weight. If the plant has outgrown its container, plan to up-pot.

issues.name: Root Rot
user_phrases: roots turning brown and slimy
smells bad in the res / rootzone
plant wilting even though roots are in water
brown mushy roots
symptoms: roots turn brown/tan, soft, slimy (healthy roots are white and firm)
foul, swampy smell from the medium or reservoir
wilting, yellowing, and stunting despite adequate water
likely_causes: oxygen-starved roots from chronic overwatering / poor drainage
warm, stagnant reservoir in hydro (low dissolved oxygen)
pathogens (e.g. Pythium) taking hold in wet, low-oxygen roots

differentiators.tell: Overwatering droop with still-white firm roots is recoverable by drying back; once roots are brown, soft, and smell, it has progressed to root rot.
In hydro, wilting while the roots sit IN water points to a root problem, not thirst — the opposite of underwatering.
Root rot yellowing comes with wilt and stinking brown roots; a plain N deficiency has healthy white roots.

clarifying_questions: What color and texture are the roots — white and firm, or brown and slimy?
Is there a foul smell, and how warm is your reservoir or medium?
issues.fix: This can kill the plant, so act promptly: improve oxygen to the roots (dry back an overwatered medium; cool and aerate a hydro reservoir), trim away mushy brown roots, and clean the system. Beneficial root inoculants can help re-establish healthy roots.

issues.name: Heat Stress
user_phrases: leaves cupping/tacoing up at the edges
leaves curling up like a canoe
top leaves curling up near the light
plant droops when it's hot
leaves pointing up and folding in near the light
symptoms: leaf edges curl/cup UPWARD ("tacoing"/"canoeing")
worst on leaves nearest the lamp or in the hottest spot
wilting during lights-on/heat; in flower can trigger foxtailing
likely_causes: canopy temperature too high (roughly >85-90 F / >30 C)
lamp too close / poor ventilation / hot tent
outdoor heat wave

differentiators.tell: Heat curls leaf EDGES up and eases as it cools; overwatering droops the whole leaf down and tracks a wet medium.
Heat tacoing can occur with a moist medium and recovers on cooling; underwatering needs actual watering to recover.
Heat is upward edge-curl tied to temperature/lamp distance; nute burn is crispy brown tips tied to feeding strength.
They overlap near the lamp and often co-occur; heat = upward curl driven by temperature, light burn = bleaching driven by raw intensity/distance.
Direction is the tell: heat curls edges UP; the nitrogen claw curls leaf tips DOWN on dark-green leaves.

clarifying_questions: What's the temperature at canopy height during lights-on?
Is it worst on the leaves closest to the light?
issues.fix: Bring canopy temperature down: raise/dim the lamp, add airflow or exhaust, or cool the space. Outdoors, provide afternoon shade and water. In flower, easing heat also prevents heat-driven foxtailing.

issues.name: Humidity Too High (Mold Risk)
user_phrases: humidity is really high in my tent
worried about mold in flower
condensation and damp air
buds staying damp
symptoms: persistently high RH (condensation, slow drying, damp canopy)
soft, lush growth; poor transpiration
conditions that invite bud rot and powdery mildew, especially in dense late flower
likely_causes: RH too high for the stage (flowering wants lower RH than veg)
poor airflow/ventilation; overcrowded canopy
large day/night temperature swings causing condensation

differentiators.tell: High humidity is the CONDITION; bud rot is the resulting infection (grey rot from inside the bud). If it's just damp air with no rot yet, you're preventing, not treating.
High humidity plus poor airflow ENABLES powdery mildew (white surface dust); the humidity itself is the risk factor, the mildew is the disease.

clarifying_questions: What's your RH and what stage/week are you in?
How's your airflow and day-vs-night temperature difference?
issues.fix: Lower RH for the stage (flowering runs drier than veg) with better ventilation, a dehumidifier, and canopy airflow; thin dense foliage and reduce temperature swings. This is mainly about preventing mold before it starts.

issues.name: Humidity Too Low / False-Deficiency from Low RH
user_phrases: air is really dry in my grow
leaves clawing and crisping but feeding is fine
seedlings/clones struggling in dry air
looks like a deficiency but nothing helps
symptoms: leaf edges curl/crisp and plants look stressed despite correct feeding and pH
increased water use / faster dry-back
seedlings and clones struggle to establish in very dry air
likely_causes: RH too low for the stage (seedlings/veg want more humidity)
heat and strong airflow drying the canopy
arid climate / winter indoor heating

differentiators.tell: If feeding strength and pH are correct but leaves still crisp, suspect low RH driving the plant to overdrink — raising humidity resolves the 'burn' without changing the feed.
Very low RH slows transpiration-driven calcium movement and mimics a calcium problem; check RH before dosing cal-mag.
Low RH doesn't just fake deficiencies, it also favors spider mites — rule out stippling/webbing under a loupe before blaming humidity alone.

clarifying_questions: What's your RH for the current stage?
Are feeding strength and pH already dialed in?
issues.fix: Raise RH toward the stage target (higher for seedlings/veg) with a humidifier, less aggressive airflow, or a humidity dome for young plants. Correct the environment before adding nutrients you don't actually need.

issues.name: Light Burn / Light Too Close
user_phrases: top leaves yellowing near the light
leaves closest to the lamp bleaching white
tops going pale but bottoms are fine
bud leaves bleaching at the top
symptoms: yellowing/bleaching on the UPPER leaves and bud tops closest to the lamp
affected leaves often stay stiff and don't wilt
sharp cutoff by distance — lower/shaded growth stays green
likely_causes: lamp too close / intensity too high for the plant
high-power LED run near max without CO2
plant grew up into the light

differentiators.tell: Direction is the tell: light burn yellows/bleaches the TOP nearest the lamp; N deficiency yellows from the BOTTOM up. Light-burned leaves also tend to stay firm rather than droop.
Light burn tracks distance from the lamp (bleached tops); nute burn tracks feeding strength (crispy tips across the plant).

They often co-occur near the lamp — light burn is bleaching from raw intensity, heat stress is upward edge-curl from temperature. Check whether it's mainly color (light) or leaf shape/temperature (heat).

clarifying_questions: Is the yellowing only on the leaves closest to the light while lower growth is fine?
How far is the lamp from the canopy, and what wattage/type?
issues.fix: Raise the lamp or dim its intensity so the top canopy isn't overexposed (check the manufacturer's hang-height/PPFD guidance). Bleached leaves won't recover their color; the goal is to stop the spread on new growth.

issues.name: Insufficient Light (Stretchy / Airy)
user_phrases: plant getting tall and stretchy
long gaps between the leaves
seedling leggy and falling over
buds airy and loose
symptoms: long internodes / stretchy, leggy growth reaching for light
thin stems; pale, sparse foliage
loose, airy, low-density buds in flower
likely_causes: light too weak or too far from the canopy
too few hours of light
plants shaded / packed together

differentiators.tell: A burst of stretch in the first ~2-3 weeks of flower is NORMAL; ongoing legginess with thin stems and wide leaf gaps in veg (or the whole plant reaching) points to too little light.
Insufficient light stretches the plant and thins growth; N deficiency yellows lower leaves without the exaggerated spacing.

clarifying_questions: What light are you running and how far from the canopy?
Is the plant stretching evenly toward the light, or just yellowing?
issues.fix: Increase usable light: move the lamp closer (within safe range), upgrade output, or extend the photoperiod for the stage. Support floppy stems and consider gentle training to even the canopy. Existing stretch stays; new growth tightens up.

issues.name: Spider Mites
user_phrases: tiny spots all over the leaves
little white/yellow dots and some webbing
fine webs between the leaves and buds
tiny moving specks under the leaves
symptoms: uniform fine STIPPLING (tiny pale/yellow dots) across the leaf, spreading upward from lower leaves
fine WEBBING between leaves/branches as populations grow
tiny moving dots on leaf undersides; heavy leaves bronze and dry
likely_causes: arrived on clones, reused soil, or from outdoors/pets
hot, dry conditions accelerating reproduction (>80 F, <50% RH)
stressed plants and dusty foliage

differentiators.tell: Mites = uniform stippling + eventual fine webbing, no black specks; thrips = irregular SILVERY streaks + black frass and NO webbing. Webbing is exclusive to mites.
Mite damage is countless tiny discrete dots (and dots move under a loupe); a deficiency is smooth areas of yellowing following leaf age, not speckling.
Low RH favors mites, so confirm with a loupe: actual stippling + moving specks means mites, not just dry-air stress.

clarifying_questions: Under a loupe on the leaf undersides, do you see tiny moving dots or fine webbing?
How hot and dry is your space, and did you recently add clones?
issues.fix: Act fast — mites explode in hot, dry rooms and can overrun a grow. Lower temperature/raise RH to slow them, treat leaf undersides on a repeat schedule to catch newly hatched mites, and isolate affected plants. Heavy infestations are serious; predatory mites are an effective option indoors.

issues.name: Thrips
user_phrases: silvery streaks on the leaves
shiny scratched-up patches like dried spit
tiny black specks on the leaves
little fast bugs on new growth
symptoms: irregular SILVERY/bronze streaks and patches (collapsed, air-filled cells)
tiny black FRASS specks near the feeding areas
slender fast-moving insects; damage favors new growth, buds, tender tissue; NO webbing
likely_causes: arrived on clones, soil, tools, or blew in outdoors
warm conditions and dense foliage
larvae on leaf undersides; pupae in the medium (why they keep returning)

differentiators.tell: Thrips = irregular silvery streaks with black frass and no webbing; mites = uniform stippling with fine webbing and no frass.
Thrips damage is random shiny scarring with black specks concentrated on new growth; a deficiency is even yellowing tied to leaf age, no metallic sheen or frass.

clarifying_questions: Are there tiny black specks (frass) near the silvery marks?
Is the damage on the newest growth, and do you see slender fast-moving insects under a loupe?
issues.fix: Confirm with the silver-streak + black-frass combo, then treat on a repeat schedule (larvae keep hatching, and pupae hide in the medium). Blue sticky traps help monitor; predatory mites/insects work indoors. Scarred leaves stay marked — watch that NEW growth stays clean.

issues.name: Fungus Gnats
user_phrases: little black flies around the soil
gnats flying up when I water
small flies crawling on the medium
seedlings stalling with flies around them
symptoms: small dark flies at the medium surface and around the pots
tiny larvae (clear/white with dark heads) in the top layer of wet medium
larvae feed on fine roots — seedlings/young plants stall or droop
likely_causes: consistently wet topsoil / overwatering
poor drainage and rich, damp organic medium
arrived in reused or contaminated soil

differentiators.tell: Gnats are a SYMPTOM of a chronically wet medium — the flies confirm the surface stays too wet. Fix the watering and you starve the gnats.
Gnats fly around the SOIL and their larvae are in the medium; thrips damage is on LEAVES (silvery streaks + frass). Different location entirely.
Both hit roots in wet conditions, but gnats leave visible flies/larvae at the surface, while root rot is brown, slimy, foul-smelling roots.

clarifying_questions: Are the flies at the soil surface (gnats) or is the damage up on the leaves?
How wet does your topsoil stay between waterings?
issues.fix: Let the top of the medium dry out between waterings — that alone breaks the cycle. Add yellow sticky traps for adults and a larvae-targeting treatment (e.g. BTi/'mosquito bits') for the soil; a dry topsoil layer or covering helps prevent re-laying.

issues.name: Aphids
user_phrases: clusters of little bugs on the stems
sticky stuff on the leaves
tiny green/black bugs on new growth
ants running up the plant
symptoms: soft-bodied insects clustered on stems, growth tips, and leaf undersides
sticky honeydew on leaves (can grow black sooty mold)
curled/distorted new growth; white cast skins; ants 'farming' them
likely_causes: blew in or arrived on new plants
tender, over-fertilized (high-N) growth attracts them
outdoor exposure; ants protecting colonies

differentiators.tell: Aphids are visible bugs in clusters plus sticky honeydew; mites are near-microscopic with stippling and webbing, no stickiness.
Aphids cluster and leave sticky honeydew; thrips leave dry silvery streaks with black frass and are slender/fast.

clarifying_questions: Do you see clustered soft bugs and any sticky residue on the leaves?
Are there ants on the plant, and is it worst on new growth?
issues.fix: Knock down populations by rinsing/wiping, then treat undersides and growth tips on a repeat schedule; control ants that protect them. Ladybugs/lacewings help outdoors. Easing high-nitrogen feeding makes growth less attractive.

issues.name: Powdery Mildew
user_phrases: white powder on the leaves
looks like flour or powdered sugar on top of the leaves
white patches spreading on the leaves
white dust that wipes off
white fuzzy patches on the stems too
symptoms: flat white/grey powdery coating on the leaf SURFACE (like flour)
starts as patches, spreads to cover leaves; favors poor airflow
wipes/rubs off (leaves a smear); can reach buds in bad cases
likely_causes: high or unstable humidity with poor air circulation
crowded canopy / stagnant air
spores introduced and given the right conditions

differentiators.tell: Under a loupe, mildew is a flat dust that lies ON the surface and wipes off; trichomes are 3D structures (a stalk with a bulbous head), sticky/sparkly, and don't rub away as powder. This is the reassurance/panic case — check before treating.
Powdery mildew is a surface coating you can see from outside; bud rot grows from INSIDE the bud (grey, mushy core) and is found by breaking the cola open.
Mildew is a powdery film; mite webbing is fine THREADS with tiny moving dots. Different texture, different cause.

clarifying_questions: Does the white wipe off as a dust, or is it sparkly/sticky and structured under a loupe?
Is it on leaf surfaces (mildew) or inside the buds (rot), and how's your humidity/airflow?
issues.fix: Treat it as a mold to control, not ignore. Improve airflow and lower humidity, remove badly affected leaves, and apply an appropriate mildew treatment early before it reaches buds. Mold on cannabis is a consumption concern, so don't smoke visibly mildewed flower.

issues.name: Bud Rot / Botrytis (Grey Mold)
user_phrases: inside of the bud is grey and mushy
bud rotting from the inside
leaves on the bud suddenly went brown/dead
fuzzy grey mold in the cola
symptoms: grey/brown fuzzy rot developing INSIDE dense buds, spreading outward
core goes mushy/slimy; a small leaf on the bud may yellow/die as an early tell
affected bud material crumbles to grey-brown; found by opening the cola
likely_causes: high humidity + poor airflow in dense late-flower buds
moisture trapped in thick colas; cool, damp conditions
rain/dew on outdoor buds

differentiators.tell: Bud rot is INSIDE the bud (grey mushy core, found by breaking it open); mildew is a white dust ON the surface. Rot destroys from within; mildew coats from without.
Fade is healthy yellowing of FAN leaves across the canopy; bud rot is a single small leaf on a bud dying while the bud beneath turns grey and soft. Check the bud interior.
Frost is sparkly, sticky, and uniform on healthy buds; rot is dull grey fuzz with mushy, discolored tissue. If it smells musty and crumbles, it's rot.

clarifying_questions: When you gently open a suspect bud, is the inside grey/brown and mushy?
What week and what's your humidity/airflow (or recent rain, if outdoors)?
issues.fix: This is serious and a consumption-safety issue — moldy cannabis should not be smoked. Remove affected buds immediately (cutting well past the rot into clean tissue), improve airflow and drop humidity, and check surrounding buds daily. In damp late flower, weigh harvesting sooner to avoid losing more.

issues.name: Damping Off (Seedlings)
user_phrases: seedling fell over and the stem pinched at the base
seedling stem went thin and dark at the soil line
sprout keeled over and died
seedlings flopping over
symptoms: stem pinches/thins and darkens right at the soil line
seedling topples over and collapses, often suddenly
usually fatal once the stem has pinched
likely_causes: overly wet medium + poor airflow (fungal)
high humidity and cool, soggy conditions
contaminated medium; overwatering young seedlings

differentiators.tell: Overwatered seedlings droop but the stem stays intact; damping off shows a pinched, thinned, darkened stem AT the soil line and the seedling falls over.
Slow-but-healthy seedlings have a firm stem and green cotyledons; damping off is a collapsing stem — sudden death, not slow progress.
Damping off is a fungal collapse at the stem base of a seedling; root rot is brown, slimy roots and can hit plants at any age.

clarifying_questions: Is the stem pinched/thin and dark right at the soil line?
How wet is the medium and how humid/cool is the space?
issues.fix: Damping off is usually fatal for the affected seedling — focus on protecting the rest: ease off water so the surface dries, improve airflow, avoid soggy cool conditions, and start in a clean, well-draining medium. Don't overwater the survivors.

issues.name: Hermaphroditism / "Nanners"
user_phrases: yellow banana things in my buds
little pollen sacs showing up
female plant growing male parts
worried my buds are going to seed
symptoms: yellow/green elongated "bananas" (stamens) emerging from within female buds
or round, ball/grape-like pollen sacs at the nodes among the flowers
risk of self-pollination and seeded buds; lowers potency/yield
likely_causes: stress (light leak in the dark period, heat, big temperature swings, major plant problems)
light burn / lamp too close
genetic instability (some strains herm readily)

differentiators.tell: Nanners/pollen sacs are the SYMPTOM; a light leak in the dark period is one of the most common CAUSES. Seeing the male parts means finding and killing the stressor (often a light leak) matters now.

clarifying_questions: Are you seeing elongated yellow 'bananas' in the buds, or round ball-like sacs at the nodes?
Any light reaching the tent during dark, recent heat spikes, or other stress?
issues.fix: Inspect daily and act fast — nanners release pollen immediately and can seed a whole room. Remove the male parts with tweezers (mist first to neutralize pollen) or isolate/remove the plant if it's widespread, then fix the stressor (check for light leaks first). Note: nanners are elongated stamens; don't confuse normal white pistils with male parts.

issues.name: Foxtailing
user_phrases: buds growing weird towers on top
spiky new growth sticking out of the buds
buds look like fox tails
elongated pointy bud growth
symptoms: calyxes stack into elongated spires/towers instead of filling into round buds
stress type: appears on the TOP buds nearest the light/heat, often with leaf tacoing or bleaching
genetic type: appears uniformly across the whole plant, gradually, on an otherwise healthy plant
likely_causes: heat stress (canopy roughly >85-90 F / >30 C)
light too intense / lamp too close
genetics (some sativa/heirloom lines foxtail naturally)

differentiators.tell: If foxtails appear only on the TOP buds near the heat and come with upward leaf-curl, it's stress-driven; correcting temperature is the fix. Whole-plant, uniform foxtailing on a healthy plant is genetic and harmless.
Stress foxtailing often rides along with bleaching on the top colas (light too close); genetic foxtailing has no bleaching or other stress signs.

clarifying_questions: Is the foxtailing only on the top buds nearest the light, or evenly across the whole plant?
Any bleaching or leaf tacoing up top, and what's your canopy temperature/lamp distance?
issues.fix: Decide genetic vs stress first. Genetic (uniform, healthy plant): nothing to fix. Stress (top-only + heat/light signs): lower canopy temperature and/or raise/dim the lamp. Existing foxtails stay; the goal is to stop new stress growth.
issues.confidence_note: Some breeders intentionally select for foxtailing, so the trait alone isn't necessarily a problem; the genetic-vs-stress read (uniform/healthy vs top-only/stressed) is what matters.

issues.name: Light Leak in Flower
user_phrases: light getting into my tent during dark
worried about a light leak in flower
buds throwing single leaves / looking weird after a light leak
timer glitched and lights came on at night
symptoms: photoperiod plants exposed to light during the dark period
can trigger hermaphroditism (nanners/pollen sacs) and seeded buds
can cause re-vegging signs (single-blade leaves, airy/odd new growth) and general stress
likely_causes: tent zippers, vents, or equipment LEDs leaking light into the dark period
timer failure / lights on at the wrong time
outdoor plants near streetlights or ambient light

differentiators.tell: Light leak is the CAUSE; herm (nanners/sacs) is one of its downstream effects. If you find nanners, checking for a dark-period light leak is the first diagnostic step.
Insufficient light causes stretchy, airy growth from too LITTLE light overall; a light leak is UNWANTED light during the dark period causing herm/re-veg — opposite problems.

clarifying_questions: Is any light reaching the plants during their dark period (zipper gaps, vents, equipment LEDs, a timer glitch)?
Are you seeing nanners/pollen sacs or odd single-blade re-veg growth?
issues.fix: Make the dark period truly dark: seal tent gaps, cover or remove stray equipment LEDs, and verify the timer. Photoperiod plants need uninterrupted darkness in flower. Then check for any herm/re-veg the leak already triggered and manage that separately.

issues.name: Transplant Shock
user_phrases: plant drooping right after I repotted it
wilted and sad after transplant
stalled out after moving to a bigger pot
looks rough a day after up-potting
symptoms: wilting/drooping and a growth pause in the day or two AFTER transplanting
temporary; typically recovers within a few days if roots weren't badly damaged
worse if roots were torn or the plant was root-bound
likely_causes: root disturbance during transplant
up-potting a root-bound plant (roots circling/matted)
big environmental change at the same time (light/temperature)

differentiators.tell: Timing is the tell — shock appears right after a transplant and recovers on its own; overwatering droop tracks a persistently wet medium unrelated to repotting.
Shock recovers within days without a moisture problem; underwatering only recovers after you actually water a dry, light pot.
Shock is tied to the recent transplant; heat stress tracks temperature/lamp distance and eases when it cools.

clarifying_questions: Did you just transplant, and was the plant root-bound or were roots disturbed?
Is the medium moisture reasonable (not soaked, not bone dry)?
issues.fix: Usually just needs time and stable, gentle conditions: keep the medium appropriately moist (not soaked), avoid stacking other stressors, and let it settle for a few days. Transplant carefully next time and up-pot before the plant gets root-bound.

issues.name: Seeds Won't Germinate / Poor Germination
user_phrases: seeds aren't sprouting
seed cracked but nothing is happening
taproot came out but it stalled
none of my seeds popped
symptoms: seeds fail to crack/sprout within the expected few days
taproot emerges but stalls or rots
sprout fails to push up and open its cotyledons
likely_causes: medium too wet (rot) or too dry (taproot dries out)
temperature too cold or too hot for germination (want warm, ~70-80 F)
planted too deep, seed handled/taproot touched, or old/low-viability seeds

differentiators.tell: Poor germination is failure to sprout in the first place; damping off is a seedling that DID sprout then collapsed at a pinched stem base.
If it has already sprouted and is just growing slowly, that's often normal early sluggishness, not a germination failure.

clarifying_questions: How long has it been, and how warm and how moist is the medium?
How deep did you plant, and are the seeds fresh or older?
issues.fix: Aim for consistently warm, lightly-moist-not-soggy conditions and shallow planting (roughly a knuckle deep); avoid touching the taproot. Give it a few days of patience. Old seeds germinate slower and less reliably. Don't let the medium swing to bone dry or waterlogged.

issues.name: Natural Late-Flower Fade
user_phrases: leaves yellowing near harvest
plant fading at the end
should I be worried leaves are dying in late flower
fan leaves going yellow as buds finish
symptoms: whole-canopy yellowing in the final ~2 weeks
fan leaves fade and drop as buds finish
likely_causes: normal senescence — the plant pulling stored nutrients into the buds

differentiators.tell: If it's the last couple weeks and buds look done/ripening, this is normal and even desirable; a problem would have started earlier and faster.
Fade is healthy yellowing of FAN leaves across the canopy; if instead a single small leaf ON a bud dies while the bud goes grey/mushy inside, that's rot, not fade — open the bud to check.

clarifying_questions: What week of flower are you in?
How do the trichomes look — clear, cloudy, amber?
issues.fix: Usually nothing — this is the plant finishing. Some growers lean into it (a light flush). Watch trichomes for harvest timing rather than the leaves.
issues.reassurance: This is normal at the end of flower — the plant is moving stored nutrients into the buds. It's not a deficiency to fix.

issues.name: Trichome Frost (Mistaken for Mold/Mildew)
user_phrases: white frosty stuff on my buds
is this mold or trichomes
sparkly white crystals on the buds
white coating on the buds, should I worry
symptoms: frosty, sparkly, crystalline coating on buds and sugar leaves
under a loupe: tiny stalks topped with bulbous, glistening heads
sticky/resinous; strain-specific aroma; uniform across healthy buds
likely_causes: normal, desirable resin production — trichomes are where cannabinoids/terpenes are made

differentiators.tell: Trichomes are 3D structures (stalk + bulbous head), sparkly and sticky, and don't wipe off as powder; mildew is a flat, dull, flour-like dust that lies on the surface and rubs off.
Frost is on the OUTSIDE, sparkly and healthy; rot is grey, dull, and mushy on the INSIDE of the bud. If it's crystalline and sticky, it's trichomes.

clarifying_questions: Under a loupe, is it sparkly with tiny stalk-and-head structures (and sticky), or a flat dull dust that wipes off?
Is the coating even and sparkly, or dull/powdery in patches?
issues.fix: Nothing to fix — frosty trichomes are a sign of a healthy, resinous, maturing plant. Use a loupe to read their color (clear/cloudy/amber) for harvest timing.
issues.reassurance: That frosty, sparkly coating is almost certainly trichomes — the resin glands you WANT. Trichomes have a stalk-and-head shape and are sticky; mildew is a flat dust that wipes off. If it's crystalline and sticky, you're looking at good, healthy buds.

issues.name: Early-Flower Stretch (Normal vs Light Problem)
user_phrases: plant shooting up fast after flip to 12/12
stretching a lot in early flower
is this stretch normal or a problem
plant doubled in height after switching to flower
symptoms: rapid vertical growth in roughly the first 2-3 weeks after flipping to flower
plant can nearly double or triple in height
even, vigorous growth with healthy leaves (not thin/leggy from reaching)
likely_causes: normal flowering stretch — plants elongate before settling into bud production

differentiators.tell: Normal stretch is vigorous, even growth in the first ~2-3 weeks of flower on a healthy plant; too-little-light stretch is thin, leggy, pale growth reaching toward the lamp and it keeps going instead of settling.

clarifying_questions: How long ago did you flip to 12/12?
Is the growth vigorous and healthy, or thin and reaching toward the light?
issues.fix: Usually nothing — plan for the height (this is expected). Manage it with light distance and optional gentle training. If growth is thin and leggy rather than vigorous, treat it as a light issue instead.
issues.reassurance: A big height burst in the first couple weeks of flower is normal — plants stretch before they bulk up buds. As long as growth is vigorous and healthy, you're fine; just leave headroom under the light.

issues.name: Seedling Slowness (Normal Early Sluggishness)
user_phrases: my seedling isn't doing much
seedling seems stuck / growing so slow
is my seedling okay, it's barely moving
first week and hardly any growth
symptoms: little visible top growth in the first week or two while roots establish
healthy green cotyledons/first leaves and a firm stem
growth accelerates once the root system develops
likely_causes: normal early establishment — seedlings invest in roots before top growth

differentiators.tell: A slow-but-healthy seedling has a moist-not-soaked medium and firm green growth; an overwatered seedling droops and sits in a constantly-wet medium.
Slowness is a healthy, firm-stemmed seedling just taking its time; damping off is a collapsing seedling with a pinched, darkened stem at the soil line.

clarifying_questions: How does the stem and the first set of leaves look — firm and green?
How wet is the medium, and how much light is it getting?
issues.fix: Usually nothing — early seedlings grow slowly while rooting in. Avoid the urge to overwater or overfeed (the most common way to actually hurt them). Give appropriate light and gentle conditions, and it'll pick up.
issues.reassurance: Slow early growth is normal — seedlings put energy into roots first, so the top can look stalled for a week or two. If the stem is firm and the leaves are green, you're fine. Don't overwater or overfeed trying to speed it up.

issues.name: When to Harvest (Trichome Reading)
user_phrases: when should I harvest
are my buds ready to chop
how do I read trichomes for harvest
clear vs cloudy vs amber, when do I cut
symptoms: deciding harvest timing by trichome color under magnification (buds, not sugar leaves)
secondary cue: pistils/hairs darkening and curling in
top colas ripen faster than lower buds
likely_causes: trichome maturity: clear = immature; cloudy/milky = peak THC; amber = THC degrading to CBN

differentiators.tell: Fading fan leaves are a rough signal that the end is near, but they don't pinpoint the window — read the trichome heads on the buds under magnification for the actual call.

clarifying_questions: Do you have a loupe or phone microscope, and what color are most trichome HEADS on the buds — clear, cloudy, or amber?
What effect are you after — more heady/uplifting or more relaxing/sedative?
issues.fix: Use 30x+ magnification on the buds (not sugar leaves). Mostly clear = wait. For a balanced result, many harvest when heads are mostly cloudy/milky with some amber; earlier/more-cloudy leans heady, later/more-amber leans sedative. Sample top vs lower canopy, since tops finish first.
issues.confidence_note: The exact cloudy-to-amber target is a matter of preference and varies by strain (some never make much amber, some go purple). Treat percentage 'rules' as guidelines and fall back on bud appearance for unusual genetics.

issues.name: Improper Drying/Curing (Hay Smell, Harshness, Jar Mold)
user_phrases: my buds smell like hay/fresh cut grass
harsh smoke after drying
buds dried too fast and smell like grass
smells like ammonia when I open the jar
symptoms: hay/fresh-cut-grass smell and harsh smoke (chlorophyll didn't break down)
over-dry, crispy buds from drying too fast/hot
in the jar: ammonia smell = too wet (mold risk); persistent hay smell = too dry / stalled cure
likely_causes: drying too fast or too hot (fan aimed at buds, warm/dry space)
jarring too wet, or not burping — traps moisture (ammonia, mold)
curing skipped or cut short; poor storage afterward

differentiators.tell: A hay/grass smell is a chlorophyll/curing problem, not mold. But a musty smell with visible grey/white fuzz inside jarred buds is actual mold — that's a consumption-safety issue, not just a bad cure.

clarifying_questions: Did the buds dry fast (a few days) or slowly (a week or so), and at what temperature/RH?
When you open the jar, is it a grassy hay smell (too dry) or a sharp ammonia smell (too wet)?
issues.fix: Dry slow and cool (roughly 60-70 F, ~50-60% RH, gentle indirect airflow) until small stems snap rather than bend. Then cure in sealed jars around 58-62% RH, burping daily for the first week or two. Ammonia in the jar means too wet — vent/dry the buds back to avoid mold. A stalled hay smell (too dry) can sometimes be eased with a humidity pack, but terpenes lost to over-drying don't return.
issues.confidence_note: Whether a pre-harvest 'flush' improves smoothness is genuinely debated among growers; the drying/curing method above matters more to hay smell than flushing does.

issues.name: Sulfur Deficiency
user_phrases: newer top leaves turning pale/yellow
upper growth going light green while bottom looks fine
young leaves yellowing evenly
new leaves pale with pinkish stems
symptoms: uniform yellowing on NEWER/upper leaves (sulfur is only semi-mobile, so it shows up top first)
whole young leaf pales fairly evenly, veins included
sometimes pink/purple tint on petioles and slowed growth
likely_causes: sulfur genuinely low in the feed/medium
pH out of range limiting sulfur uptake (lockout, not a true shortage)
heavy leaching / very lean medium

differentiators.tell: Location is the tell: nitrogen yellows OLDER/lower leaves first and climbs; sulfur pales the NEWER/upper leaves first because it moves less freely.
Mg is interveinal (green veins, yellow between) on older/mid leaves; sulfur is fairly UNIFORM yellowing on younger leaves.
If feed already contains sulfur but it keeps spreading, check pH before adding more — an off pH can lock sulfur out.

clarifying_questions: Is the yellowing worst on the NEW top growth or the OLD bottom growth?
What are you feeding, and do you know your runoff/reservoir pH?
issues.fix: Confirm pH is in range first so you're not chasing lockout. If sulfur is genuinely low, many complete base nutrients and cal-mag/Epsom-type products supply it — move toward label strength and recheck new growth in a few days.
issues.confidence_note: True sulfur deficiency is fairly uncommon with complete nutrients; pale new growth is more often pH or another micronutrient, so rule those out first.

issues.name: Zinc Deficiency
user_phrases: new leaves yellowing between the veins and looking crinkled
top growth bunched up with short spacing
small twisted new leaves
new growth pale and distorted
symptoms: interveinal chlorosis (yellow between green veins) on NEW/upper leaves
shortened internodes — new growth bunches into a tight rosette
small, distorted, sometimes twisted or wrinkled new leaves
likely_causes: high root-zone pH locking out zinc (very common trigger)
zinc genuinely low in the feed
cold/wet medium reducing micronutrient uptake

differentiators.tell: Iron gives clean interveinal yellowing on new leaves with normal shape; zinc ADDS shortened internodes and small, distorted/twisted new growth.
Mn interveinal chlorosis carries scattered brown necrotic flecks; zinc leans toward distortion and tight, stacked new growth instead.
Zinc locks out at HIGH pH — pale, bunched new tops with high runoff/res pH is usually lockout, so fix pH before dosing zinc.

clarifying_questions: Is the new growth also bunched up with very short spacing between leaves?
What's your runoff/reservoir pH?
issues.fix: Check and correct pH first (zinc locks out when pH runs high) — that resolves most cases. If it persists in range, a complete micronutrient supplement supplies zinc; damaged leaves won't recover but new growth should normalize.

issues.name: Manganese Deficiency
user_phrases: yellowing between veins on new leaves with brown spots
new growth mottled with little dead specks
upper leaves yellow between veins and spotting
speckled yellowing near the top
symptoms: interveinal chlorosis on NEWER/upper leaves with veins staying green
scattered small brown necrotic spots/flecks develop within the yellow areas
starts near the base of the leaf and spreads outward
likely_causes: high pH locking out manganese
manganese genuinely low in the feed
over-liming / very alkaline medium

differentiators.tell: Iron is cleaner interveinal yellowing with few or no spots; manganese adds distinctive small brown necrotic FLECKS inside the yellow zones.
Zinc distorts new growth and shortens internodes; manganese keeps leaf shape more normal but adds the spotting.
Mg hits OLDER/mid leaves; manganese hits NEWER/upper leaves — location separates them.

clarifying_questions: Are the yellow areas on new leaves developing tiny brown dead spots?
What's your runoff/reservoir pH?
issues.fix: Correct pH into range first (a high pH is the usual cause). If it continues in range, a complete micronutrient product supplies manganese. Avoid overcorrecting — excess manganese can itself cause problems.

issues.name: Boron Deficiency
user_phrases: new growth tips looking twisted and brittle
growing tips turning brown and dying
new leaves thick, rough, deformed
top shoots stunted and gnarly
symptoms: abnormal, thick, brittle, twisted NEW growth
brown/necrotic or dying growing tips (terminal shoots)
rough or corky stems; new leaves may be misshapen
likely_causes: boron genuinely low in the feed/water
low humidity or inconsistent watering reducing boron uptake (it moves with transpiration)
pH out of range affecting availability

differentiators.tell: Both damage new growth, but calcium tends to give brown SPOTS and hooked/curled tips; boron leans toward brittle, thick, deformed shoots and dead growing points.
An off pH mimics boron symptoms — check and correct pH before dosing boron, which is easy to overdo.
Broad/russet mites also twist and glaze new growth, but that's a moving pest problem — inspect at 60x+; a nutrient issue has no mites.

clarifying_questions: Is it mainly the growing TIPS that are deformed/dying, and how's your humidity and watering consistency?
What's your pH, and have you checked new growth under magnification for mites?
issues.fix: Confirm pH and keep watering/humidity steady so boron can move into new growth. If genuinely deficient, correct with a complete micronutrient source and go LIGHT — boron toxicity happens quickly, so under-correct rather than over.
issues.confidence_note: Boron deficiency is relatively rare and easily confused with calcium issues or mite damage; because boron toxicity is easy to trigger, rule out pH and pests before supplementing.

issues.name: Copper Deficiency
user_phrases: new leaves very dark with a bluish or metallic sheen
leaf tips and edges going dark and dying on new growth
top leaves twisting and wilting for no clear reason
dark shiny leaves that droop
symptoms: new/upper leaves unusually dark green with a blue/metallic or purple undertone
leaf tips and margins darken/necrose; leaves may twist or wilt
slowed growth with a stiff, shiny appearance
likely_causes: copper genuinely low (uncommon with complete nutrients)
pH out of range limiting copper uptake
excess of other elements antagonizing copper

differentiators.tell: Overwatering droops the whole plant with a constantly-wet medium; copper deficiency shows dark, shiny, twisting NEW leaves with darkened tips regardless of soil moisture.
Both give dark leaves, but nitrogen toxicity claws the leaf tips DOWN on glossy green leaves; copper adds a bluish/metallic cast plus dying tips/margins on new growth.
An off pH mimics micronutrient shortages — correct pH before assuming a true copper shortage.

clarifying_questions: Is the dark, shiny look on the NEW top growth, with tips/edges dying back?
What's your pH, and are you running a complete micronutrient feed?
issues.fix: Check pH first — genuine copper deficiency is rare, and lockout is the more common cause. A complete micronutrient product supplies copper; go light, since copper is toxic in excess.
issues.confidence_note: Copper deficiency is quite rare in practice; suspect pH, overwatering, or another cause first and confirm before adding copper (which is easily toxic).

issues.name: Molybdenum Deficiency
user_phrases: middle leaves yellowing with orange or pink edges
leaves turning yellow then getting reddish margins
mottled yellow-orange on mid-plant leaves
looks like nitrogen deficiency but with orange tints
symptoms: yellowing that often starts on middle-aged leaves and can spread
orange/pink/reddish mottling or margins developing on affected leaves
can look like a nitrogen problem because molybdenum is tied to nitrogen use
likely_causes: LOW pH locking out molybdenum (its classic trigger)
molybdenum genuinely low (rare)
very acidic medium overall

differentiators.tell: Plain nitrogen shortage is uniform yellowing from the bottom up; molybdenum adds orange/pink mottling and is usually a LOW-pH lockout rather than a true shortage.
Molybdenum specifically locks out at LOW pH — acidic runoff/res with these symptoms points to correcting pH up rather than dosing Mo.
P deficiency purples/bronzes older leaves with dull dark tone; molybdenum trends toward orange/pink mottling tied to a low pH.

clarifying_questions: Is your runoff/reservoir pH running low (acidic)?
Are the affected leaves developing orange/pink tints along with the yellowing?
issues.fix: Check pH first and raise it into range if it's too acidic — that resolves most molybdenum cases, since it's almost always a low-pH lockout rather than a real shortage. Complete nutrients supply the small amount needed.
issues.confidence_note: Molybdenum deficiency is rare and almost always a low-pH lockout; correcting pH is the primary fix.

issues.name: Cold Stress / Low Temperature
user_phrases: leaves and stems turning purple in cold weather
growing slow and drooping when it's cold
purpling since temps dropped at night
leaves curling and dark in a cold tent
symptoms: purple/red/blue hues in leaves, stems, and petioles, often worse after cold nights
slowed growth, drooping, and sometimes leaf curl in cold conditions
in flower, cool nights can deepen bud color but also slow ripening
likely_causes: canopy/room temperature too low (especially night lows toward or below ~50-60 F / 10-15 C)
large day-to-night temperature swings
cold medium/root zone slowing uptake

differentiators.tell: P purpling comes with dull, dark, sometimes spotted leaves and poor growth regardless of temperature; cold purpling tracks the COLD and often eases when you warm the space.
Genetic color shows on an otherwise vigorous, healthy plant; cold purpling pairs with slowed growth, drooping, and a genuinely cold environment.
Nitrogen yellows lower leaves from the bottom up; cold stress trends purple/red with sluggish growth, not uniform yellowing.

clarifying_questions: What are your temperatures, especially at night / lights-off?
Did the purpling start when it got colder, and is overall growth slow?
issues.fix: Raise temperatures into a comfortable range and reduce the day-to-night swing — insulate the space, warm the room, or lift pots off cold floors. Growth and color usually recover as it warms; cold-driven purpling on a healthy plant is cosmetic.

issues.name: Wind Burn (Fan Too Close)
user_phrases: leaves clawing and curling right where the fan hits
leaves near the fan look burnt and twisted
curling leaves only on one side facing the fan
wind blowing hard and leaves canoeing
symptoms: clawing/curling and 'canoeing' leaves concentrated where airflow hits hardest
dried, bronzed, or tattered leaf edges in the fan's direct path
damage localized to the wind path rather than spread by leaf age
likely_causes: a fan aimed directly at the canopy on high, hitting the same spot constantly
too much direct airflow for the plant's size
leaves whipped continuously against each other or hardware

differentiators.tell: The nitrogen claw hits dark-green upper growth broadly; wind burn is LOCALIZED to wherever the fan blasts and tracks airflow, not feeding.
Heat tacoing is worst near the LAMP/hottest spot; wind burn is worst in the direct FAN path — follow which one lines up with the damage.
Nute burn is crispy brown TIPS tied to feed strength across the plant; wind burn is curling/tattering confined to the airflow path.

clarifying_questions: Is the damage concentrated exactly where a fan blows on the plant?
Are your fans aimed straight at the canopy, and on how high a setting?

warm conditions and crowded, poorly ventilated canopy
nearby infested houseplants or garden

differentiators.tell: Gnats are dark, hang around the SOIL surface, and fly weakly; whiteflies are white, cluster UNDER leaves, and lift off in a cloud when you shake the plant.
Aphids are soft-bodied and stay put in clusters; whiteflies are winged and take flight — both leave honeydew, but only whiteflies scatter into the air.

Are leaf undersides where you see them, and is there sticky residue?
issues.fix: Isolate affected plants and hit the leaf undersides on a repeat schedule to catch newly hatched adults. Yellow sticky traps help monitor and knock down fliers, and improving airflow makes the environment less favorable.

distorted new growth and nothing shows under a normal loupe

spread by handling, clothing, or tools between plants
warm conditions accelerating reproduction

Can you inspect the growing tips at 60x or higher, and did you recently bring in clones?
issues.fix: Treat as serious — these spread fast and hide. Isolate affected plants immediately, sanitize hands/tools between plants, and run an aggressive REPEAT treatment schedule targeting new growth; predatory mites and appropriate miticides are common options. Confirmation often needs high magnification or a lab.
issues.confidence_note: Broad and russet mites are notoriously hard to see; diagnosis is often made from the distinctive distortion/bronzing pattern plus high-magnification inspection.

issues.confidence_note: Several root/vascular pathogens look alike; definitive identification usually needs a lab, but the management (remove, sanitize, don't reuse soil) is similar.

issues.name: Hop Latent Viroid (HLVd / "Dudding")

possible spread through root contact/shared water

differentiators.tell: Deficiencies show characteristic leaf patterns and respond to correcting feed/pH; HLVd stunting/dudding persists across a clean, dialed-in grow and often runs in a whole clone line from one mother.

issues.fix: There's no cure — the priority is confirmation and containment. A lab PCR test is the reliable diagnosis, since symptoms overlap with ordinary stress and carriers can look normal. Cull or isolate infected mothers, sterilize blades/tools between every plant, and rebuild from tested-clean stock.
issues.confidence_note: HLVd cannot be reliably diagnosed by eye — symptoms mimic many stressors and infected plants are often symptomless carriers; lab testing is the standard for confirmation.

Is the new growth leafy and smooth-edged (veg-like), rather than pollen sacs?

issues.name: Small Autoflower / Compact Plant (Normal Genetics)
